native_result.query: Does increased time preference leads to higher BMI?
native_result.HypoA: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Fit an OLS Regression Model
native_result.HypoB: In the NLSY79 cohort, individuals who show more impatient time preference — operationalized as putting less money into savings in 1989 — tend to have higher BMI: savers have about 0.3–0.4 lower BMI units than non-savers after covariate adjustment (adjusted β = −0.39, p = 0.001 for the saver indicator; put-in vs took-out contrast β = −0.35, p = 0.011), and greater net savings flow predicts significantly less BMI growth from 1981 to 1989 (adjusted β = −0.017 per log-dollar, p = 0.008; −0.19 BMI units per IQR). The association does not persist in the 1992−1989 change window and is null for the raw dollar-denominated flow, so support is directional and modest. This is a correlational, proxy-based association (the dataset has no direct time-preference measure): savings also reflect income and liquidity, reverse causality (health affecting saving) cannot be excluded, the pooled sample includes non-representative NLSY79 oversamples, and attrition reaches 30% by 1992 — so the hypothesis is that impatient time preference is ASSOCIATED with higher BMI, not that it causally raises BMI.
native_result.WorkflowB: analysis/solution.py: (1) load 12,686×61 NLSY79 extract; (2) convert 1981 feet-inches height codes to inches (verified against 1985 inches), trim 48–84 in; (3) read weights as pounds→kg (primary; literal-kg sensitivity included), trim 70–500 lb, BMI = kg/m² with 15–60 plausibility bounds; (4) build 1989 time-preference proxy from savings: net flow (put−out, winsorized at $100k), 4-category ordinal, log-symmetric flow, with category-consistency validation; (5) OLS with HC1 SEs — unadjusted and adjusted cross-sectional BMI 1989 models, 4-category contrast (ref = took money out), and within-person first-difference models ΔBMI(89−81) and ΔBMI(92−89) with baseline BMI; covariates: sex, race/ethnicity, age, education, parents' education, family size, family income (topcode-aware), log net wealth, incarceration (Jail residence) indicator; (6) attrition/covariate-balance diagnostics and literal-kg sensitivity; outputs in analysis/results.json.

sub_hypo.text: In the NLSY79 cohort, greater impatience, proxied by putting less money into savings in 1989, is associated with higher BMI in 1989: savers have approximately 0.3–0.4 lower BMI units than non-savers after covariate adjustment.
sub_hypo.context: Pooled NLSY79 sample, including non-representative oversamples. BMI uses 1981 height converted to inches and weights interpreted primarily as pounds and converted to kilograms; height, weight, and BMI plausibility bounds are 48–84 inches, 70–500 pounds, and 15–60, respectively. Adjusted OLS models use HC1 standard errors and control for sex, race/ethnicity, age, education, parents' education, family size, family income with topcode awareness, log net wealth, and jail-residence incarceration status. Savings are a proxy, not a direct time-preference measure.
